title: Asking the way — prepositions that become endings
title_target: ডাকঘর কোন দিকে? — Dak-ghôr kon di-ké?
goal: Ask for and follow directions, and master the place words that all demand a possessive ending on the noun before them: বাড়ির সামনে, টেবিলের উপরে.
bekal: ask the way with কোন দিকে and কতদূর
use সামনে, পিছনে, উপরে, নিচে, ভিতরে, পাশে with the ending -র · -এর
tell the -এ that means “at” from the -এ that means “to”
use থেকে for “from” in both place and time

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Lost near the market
dialogs.intro: Ani is looking for the post office and has taken three wrong turns. She stops at a tea stall and asks the owner. Notice that every place word — সামনে, পিছনে, পাশে — is always preceded by a noun that already carries the possessive ending.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Excuse me, brother, just a moment. Which way is the post office?
lines.literal: brother, a-little — listen. post-office — which — direction-to?

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: The post office? Go straight, then right.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: How far is it? Can I walk?

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: Very close. Five minutes. Next to the bank.
lines.literal: very — near. five — minute. bank-'s — side-at.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Next to the bank? I haven't seen a bank.

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: Behind that big tree. The rickshaws wait under the tree.
lines.literal: that — big — tree-the-'s — behind-at. tree-'s — under-at — rickshaw — stands.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I see. And how do I get there from the market?
lines.literal: have-understood. and — market — from — how — will-go?

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: Don't go into the market. Go around the outside, to the left.
lines.literal: market-'s — inside-to — will-enter — not. outside — via — left-to.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: OK. What time does the post office close?

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: At four. It's three now, so hurry.
lines.literal: four-o'clock-at. now — three-o'clock — strikes, quickly — go.

lines.speaker: দোকানি:
lines.id: Oh, don't mention it. Stop for some tea on your way back!
lines.literal: oh, anything — mind-in — will-do — not. returning-'s — way-on — tea — having-drunk — will-go!

notes: **Bengali place words demand a possessive ending before them.** You can't say *বাড়ি সামনে*; the correct form is **বাড়ির সামনে** — literally “house-'s front-at”. Likewise টেবিলের উপরে (on the table), গাছের নিচে (under the tree), ব্যাংকের পাশে (next to the bank). ⚠️ Once you realize these words are really **nouns** — সামনে means “the front”, নিচে means “the underside” — the pattern makes sense: you're saying “the front of the house”, just as English does with *in front of*.

⚠️ **One ending for both “at” and “to”.** আমি ঢাকায় আছি means “I'm **in** Dhaka”; আমি ঢাকায় যাই means “I go **to** Dhaka”. The ending is identical. Only the verb decides: থাকা · আছা call for “at/in”, while যাওয়া · আসা call for “to”. English uses two words; Bengali leaves the choice to the verb.

**থেকে means “from” for both place and time.** ঢাকা থেকে (from Dhaka), সকাল থেকে (since morning), ছটা থেকে (from six o'clock). ⚠️ থেকে stands **after** its noun with no possessive ending — unlike সামনে and পাশে, which demand one. The reason: থেকে isn't a noun but a pure postposition.

**দিকে means “toward” and is used for a direction, not necessarily the final destination.** কোন দিকে? (which way?), বাজারের দিকে (toward the market), ডান দিকে (to the right). You'll hear this word constantly from rickshaw drivers.

⚠️ **“Five minutes” almost never means five minutes.** In Bengal, as in many places, খুব কাছে (very close) and পাঁচ মিনিট are polite ways of saying “not too far, don't worry”. If the distance matters, ask **কত মিনিট হেঁটে?** (how many minutes on foot?) — or better yet, show the map on your phone.

**কিছু মনে করবেন না** *ki-chhu mô-né kôr-bèn na* is one of the most useful sentences in Bengali. Literally “don't take anything to heart”, it can mean “no problem”, “no offense”, or “sorry to bother you” — depending on when you say it. Keep it handy; it rescues many awkward moments.

**An invitation to “stop for tea” is not empty politeness.** If someone who just gave you directions invites you for tea, they mean it — and accepting now and then is the fastest way to actually practice the language. ⚠️ You don't have to pay; declining politely is fine too, but do it with a smile and **পরে আসব** (I'll come later).

after: **Without a possessive ending, these postpositions follow the noun directly:** … **থেকে** (from), … **পর্যন্ত** (until, as far as), … **দিয়ে** (via, with), … **ছাড়া** (without), … **সঙ্গে · সাথে** (together with). ⚠️ সঙ্গে actually takes the ending too — আমার সঙ্গে (with me) — so learn it with the first group.

grammars.title: Directions
after: ⚠️ **ডান and বাম are adjectives; ডানে and বামে already carry the -এ ending.** That's why কোন দিকে is দিক + এ. To say “the right side of the road”, the order is **রাস্তার ডান দিকে** — possessive on the road, then ডান, then দিকে.

sections.title: Taking a rickshaw and a bus

blocks.text: The রিকশা, a pedal rickshaw, is the backbone of Bengal's cities, and agreeing on the fare **before you get in** is a must. Once you're seated, the price is no longer up for negotiation.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: Will you go to the post office?

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three things to know before you get in
items: **Destination first, price second.** The natural order: “ডাকঘর যাবেন?” → “কত নেবেন?” → bargain → “চলুন”. Asking the price before the destination just confuses the driver.
**Rickshaw drivers often don't know building names, but they know intersections.** Naming the nearest মোড় — “নিউমার্কেট মোড়” — works far better than naming a shop.

**City buses don't always come to a full stop.** Shout **নামব** (*nam-bô* — I'll get off) before your stop, and the conductor will shout back. If in doubt, tell the passenger next to you where you're going; someone almost always looks after you until you get off.

blocks.text: A word about addresses. Addresses in Dhaka and Kolkata often run from **small to large**: house number, road number, neighborhood, city — for example ৭ নম্বর রোড, ধানমন্ডি, ঢাকা. That's the same order as an English address, so reading one won't confuse you. What does confuse people is that one neighborhood can have several roads with the same number; that's why everyone gives a **ল্যান্ডমার্ক** — a mosque, a big tree, or a well-known shop — as the final pointer.

ডাকঘর কোন দিকে? — সোজা যান, তারপর বামে। — কতদূর? — বইটা টেবিলের উপরে। — আমি পথ হারিয়েছি। — এখানে থামুন ভাই।
